questions.question: Explain why the Soviet Union was weakened by the early 1980s.
questions.expected_answer: A stagnating centrally planned economy (shortages, poor-quality goods, technology lag, grain imports); the arms race took a much larger share of a smaller economy (perhaps 15-25% of output); the Afghanistan war from 1979 (about 15 000 Soviet dead, ended February 1989); Reagan's military build-up and SDI (1983); falling oil prices in the mid-1980s; ageing leaders (Brezhnev d. 1982, Andropov, Chernenko).

questions.question: Describe Gorbachev's reforms and how they changed relations with the West and Eastern Europe.
questions.expected_answer: Gorbachev (leader from March 1985) introduced glasnost (openness: free speech, criticism, release of prisoners; Chernobyl 1986) and perestroika (economic restructuring, some private enterprise). New thinking in foreign policy: summits with Reagan (Geneva 1985, Reykjavik 1986), INF Treaty (December 1987), withdrawal from Afghanistan (1989), UN speech (December 1988) cutting 500 000 troops; the Brezhnev Doctrine was abandoned (the Sinatra Doctrine), so Eastern Europe could choose its own way.

questions.question: Explain how and why the Berlin Wall was opened in 1989, and its consequences, including for South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Poland elected Solidarity (June 1989); Hungary opened its border (September 1989) and East Germans fled; Leipzig Monday marches (70 000 on 9 October); Honecker resigned (18 October); half a million protested in East Berlin (4 November). On 9 November Schabowski announced travel rules "immediately"; crowds gathered and guards opened the gates. Consequences: Velvet Revolution, Malta summit (December 1989), German reunification (3 October 1990), USSR's collapse (1991). South Africa: the total onslaught argument collapsed, the ANC lost Soviet backing; de Klerk unbanned movements on 2 February 1990, alongside internal resistance and sanctions.
